analysis.one_liner: Ends new coal, oil, and gas leasing on federal land and offshore waters and cancels Arctic-area leases.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in a House subcommittee from June 2021 until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar the Interior Department from issuing, renewing, extending, or reoffering any lease for coal, oil, tar sands, oil shale, or gas on federal land, and would block all new offshore oil and gas leases in the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic, Pacific, and Arctic oceans. It would also cancel within 60 days existing offshore leases in the Beaufort Sea, Cook Inlet, and Chukchi Sea. Narrow exceptions allow action during an imminent national security threat or where canceling a pre-existing lease would breach its contract. The bill's stated goal is to keep federal fossil fuels, which it says account for a large share of potential emissions, from being extracted and burned.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people exposed to climate change, air pollution near federal drilling, and coastal communities facing offshore spill risk; also renewable energy industries competing for the same land and capital.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal communities and people exposed to pollution

how_it_helps.text: The bill would stop all new federal fossil fuel leasing onshore and on the outer Continental Shelf, which the findings say would prevent the release of 90 percent of the potential emissions from federal fossil fuels [S3].
It would cancel existing offshore leases in the Beaufort Sea, Cook Inlet, and Chukchi Sea within 60 days, ending drilling plans in Arctic and Alaska waters [S2][S3].
It would extend the ban to renewals, extensions, and reoffers of expiring leases, so companies could not simply roll over existing lease holdings indefinitely [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and coal companies that lease federal land and waters, plus workers and state and local governments that depend on federal-lease royalties and drilling jobs.

drawbacks.text: Ending new federal leases would cut royalty payments that the federal government shares with states and that fund schools and local services in energy-producing regions [S3].

The bill would not touch leases already in production, so existing drilling would continue and near-term emissions would fall little; the climate benefit depends on how much future production comes from new leases [S3].
Restricting supply could raise energy prices for consumers and cost jobs in Gulf Coast, Rocky Mountain, and coal communities, a cost an honest supporter must weigh against the climate gains [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The climate case is real but partial: blocking new leases stops future expansion of drilling on public land, yet producing leases are untouched and companies already hold large reserves, so the biggest effect is on the pace of new extraction decades out. The costs fall concentrated and fast — royalties, jobs, and energy prices — while the benefits are diffuse and slow. The narrow exceptions for national security and contract breaches limit the risk of sudden supply shocks.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Natural Resources Committee and then to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee in June 2021, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jared Huffman introduced the bill on April 14, 2021, with 15 original cosponsors including Natural Resources Committee Chairman Raúl Grijalva [S1][S3].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Natural Resources, and on June 8, 2021, to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources [S5].
The bill gathered 33 cosponsors, all Democrats [S4].
No further action was recorded; the bill remained in subcommittee until the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel companies holding federal leases and the leasing status quo: nothing changed, so drilling and leasing on federal land and waters continued under existing law, and no hearing ever tested the bill's claims or its opponents'.

sides.party_line_note: All 33 cosponsors plus the sponsor were Democrats, and no floor vote ever occurred to test whether any Republicans would support it [S4].

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers on federal land and offshore
industries.note: The bill would end all new federal onshore and offshore leasing and cancel Arctic-area leases, cutting off the industry's cheapest long-run source of new acreage. Its gain from the bill's defeat is continued access to publicly owned resources that the bill's findings frame as a major source of climate emissions [S3].
The bill would bar any new coal lease sale or lease renewal on federal land subject to the Mineral Leasing Act, blocking the main channel for expanding federal coal mining [S3].

industries.industry: Tar sands and oil shale developers
industries.note: These unconventional fuels are explicitly named in the leasing ban; federal leasing is their main pathway to commercial-scale development [S3].
Blocking new fossil fuel leases on the same federal land shifts federal energy development toward wind, solar, and transmission projects competing for that acreage and capital [S3].
